metadata.title: A New Class of Alternating Proximal Minimization Algorithms with Costs-to-Move

items.name: Algorithm (CA²)
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be abstract spaces. Let $f: \mathcal{X} \mapsto \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$, $g: \mathcal{Y} \mapsto \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be objective functions. Let $h: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^{+} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be the cost to change on $\mathcal{X}$, $k: \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^{+} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be the cost to change on $\mathcal{Y}$, and $c: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^+$ be a coupling function. Let $\alpha_n, \beta_n, \mu_n, \nu_n$ be nonnegative parameters. Given $(x_0, y_0) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, the cognitive alternating algorithm $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$ generates $(x_n, y_n) \to (x_{n+1}, y_n) \to (x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})$ as follows:

$$
(\mathrm{CA}^2) \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
x_{n+1} \in \operatorname{argmin} \{f(\xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi): \xi \in \mathcal{X}\}, \\
y_{n+1} \in \operatorname{argmin} \{g(\eta) + \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, \eta) + \nu_n k(y_n, \eta): \eta \in \mathcal{Y}\}.
\end{array} \right.
$$

items.name: Definition 1.1
items.statement:
Given nonnegative constants $\alpha, \beta, \mu, \nu$, an inertial Nash equilibrium, in short $\mathrm{INE}(\alpha, \beta, \mu, \nu)$, is defined as a couple $(\overline{x}, \overline{y}) \in \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ such that

- $\overline{x} \in \arg\min\{f(\xi) + \beta c(\xi, \overline{y}) + \alpha h(\overline{x}, \xi) : \xi \in \mathcal{X}\}$,
- $\overline{y} \in \arg\min\{g(\eta) + \mu c(\overline{x}, \eta) + \nu k(\overline{y}, \eta) : \eta \in \mathcal{Y}\}$.

items.name: Resolvent (Proximal) Operator
items.statement:
For a convex, proper, lower semicontinuous function $\varphi: \mathcal{H} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and a parameter $\lambda > 0$, the resolvent (or proximal) operator is defined by

$$
J_{\lambda}^{\partial\varphi}(x) = (I + \lambda \partial\varphi)^{-1}(x) = \operatorname{argmin}_{\xi \in \mathcal{H}}\left\{\varphi(\xi) + \frac{1}{2\lambda}\|\xi - x\|^2\right\}.
$$

In this paper, the notation $T_f^n = (I + \frac{1}{\alpha_n+\beta}\partial f)^{-1}$ and $T_g^n = (I + \frac{1}{\mu+\nu_n}\partial g)^{-1}$ is used.

items.name: Firmly Nonexpansive Operator
items.statement:
An operator $T: \mathcal{H} \to \mathcal{H}$ on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ is firmly nonexpansive if

$$
\langle T x - T x', x - x' \rangle \geq \|T x - T x'\|^2 \qquad \forall x, x' \in \mathcal{H}.
$$

Equivalently, $T$ is firmly nonexpansive iff $T = \frac{1}{2}(I + N)$ for some nonexpansive operator $N$.

items.name: Monotonicity-Adjusting Factor δ_n
Separately Continuous Function
items.statement: A function $F: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}$ on topological spaces $\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}$ is separately continuous if for each fixed $y \in \mathcal{Y}$, the map $x \mapsto F(x, y)$ is continuous on $\mathcal{X}$, and for each fixed $x \in \mathcal{X}$, the map $y \mapsto F(x, y)$ is continuous on $\mathcal{Y}$.

items.name: ε-argmin (ε-Approximate Minimizer)
items.statement:
For a function $\varphi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, the set of $\varepsilon$-approximate minimizers is defined by

$$
\varepsilon\text{-}\operatorname{argmin}_{\xi \in \mathcal{X}} \varphi(\xi) = \{x \in \mathcal{X}: \varphi(x) \leq \inf_{\mathcal{X}} \varphi + \varepsilon\}.
$$

items.name: Algorithm (ACA²)
items.statement:
The approximate version of $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$, denoted $(\mathrm{ACA}^2)$, with tolerance $\varepsilon_n > 0$, is:

$$
(\mathrm{ACA}^2) \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
x_{n+1} \in \varepsilon_n\text{-argmin} \{f(\xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi): \xi \in \mathcal{X}\}, \\
y_{n+1} \in \varepsilon_n\text{-argmin} \{g(\eta) + \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, \eta) + \nu_n k(y_n, \eta): \eta \in \mathcal{Y}\}.
\end{array} \right.
$$

items.name: Remark 1
items.statement:
When $\alpha = \nu = 0$, one recovers the usual notion of Nash equilibrium:

- $\overline{x} \in \arg\min\{F(\xi, \overline{y}) : \xi \in \mathcal{X}\}$,
- $\overline{y} \in \arg\min\{G(\overline{x}, \eta) : \eta \in \mathcal{Y}\}$,

where $F(\xi, \eta) = f(\xi) + \beta c(\xi, \eta)$, $G(\xi, \eta) = g(\eta) + \mu c(\xi, \eta)$.

items.name: Lemma 2.3
items.proof:
Set $\xi = x_n$ and $\eta = y_n$ in the defining inequalities of $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$; sequences $x_n$ and $y_n$ verify

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \leq f(x_n) + \beta_n c(x_n, y_n), \\
g(y_{n+1}) + \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) + \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1}) \leq g(y_n) + \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n).
\end{array} \right.
$$

Multiplying the first inequality by $\mu_n$ and the second one by $\beta_n$ we obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l}
[\mu_n f(x_{n+1})] + [\mu_n \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1})] + [\mu_n \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n)] \\
\leq [\mu_n f(x_n) + \mu_n \beta_n c(x_n, y_n)]
\end{array}
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{l}
[\beta_n g(y_{n+1}) + \beta_n \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})] + [\beta_n \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1})] \\
\leq [\beta_n g(y_n)] + [\beta_n \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n)].
\end{array}
$$

Add the two inequalities to get (2.4). [Adding yields: $\mu_n f(x_{n+1}) + \beta_n g(y_{n+1}) + \mu_n \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1}) + \mu_n \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) + \beta_n \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) \leq \mu_n f(x_n) + \beta_n g(y_n) + \mu_n \beta_n c(x_n, y_n) + \beta_n \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n)$. Canceling the common term $\mu_n \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n)$ from both sides yields (2.4).]

items.name: Theorem 2.4
items.proof:
Dividing inequality (2.4) by $\beta_n \equiv \mu_n$, we obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l}
[f(x_{n+1}) + g(y_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})] + [\alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1})] \\
\leq [f(x_n) + g(y_n) + \beta_n c(x_n, y_n)].
\end{array}
$$

Since $\beta_n$ is nonincreasing, we may replace $\beta_n$ with $\beta_{n+1}$ in the left-hand member [because $\beta_n \geq \beta_{n+1}$ and $c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) \geq 0$, we have $\beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) \geq \beta_{n+1} c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})$, so the inequality is preserved with the smaller coefficient],

$$
\begin{array}{l}
[f(x_{n+1}) + g(y_{n+1}) + \beta_{n+1} c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})] + [\alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1})] \\
\leq [f(x_n) + g(y_n) + \beta_n c(x_n, y_n)],
\end{array}
$$

which shows that the quantity $f(x_n) + g(y_n) + \beta_n c(x_n, y_n)$ is nonincreasing; as it is nonnegative it is convergent [being a nonincreasing sequence bounded below by $0$, it converges to its infimum], which proves point (a).

Summing the inequality above from $n = 0$ to $N$, we obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{n=0}^{N}[\alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1})] \\
\leq [f(x_0) + g(y_0) + \beta_0 c(x_0, y_0)] - [f(x_{N+1}) + g(y_{N+1}) + \beta_{N+1} c(x_{N+1}, y_{N+1})] \\
\leq [f(x_0) + g(y_0) + \beta_0 c(x_0, y_0)] - [\inf_{\mathcal{X}} f + \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g],
\end{array}
$$

which proves point (b).

items.name: Theorem 2.5
items.proof:
Divide inequality (2.4) in Lemma 2.3 by $\delta_n$, and display positive quantities like $f(x_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f$ and $g(y_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g$. [Subtracting $(\mu_n/\delta_n)\inf_{\mathcal{X}}f + (\beta_n/\delta_n)\inf_{\mathcal{Y}}g$ from both sides yields the same inequality with $f(\cdot) - \inf f$ and $g(\cdot) - \inf g$, since these constants are independent of $n$ and thus preserve the inequality direction.] Then

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left[\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}\left(f(x_{n+1}) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\right) + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\left(g(y_{n+1}) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g\right) + \frac{\beta_n \mu_n}{\delta_n} c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\right] \\
+ \left[\frac{\mu_n \alpha_n}{\delta_n} h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \frac{\beta_n \nu_n}{\delta_n} k(y_n, y_{n+1})\right] \\
\leq \left[\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}\bigg(f(x_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\bigg) + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\left(g(y_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g\right) + \frac{\beta_n \mu_n}{\delta_n} c(x_n, y_n)\right].
\end{array}
$$

Each sequence $\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}$, $\frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}$, and $\frac{\beta_n \mu_n}{\delta_n}$ is nonincreasing [verification by cases: (Case 1: β_n↓, μ_n↓) δ_n=1 ⇒ μ_n/δ_n=μ_n↓, β_n/δ_n=β_n↓, β_nμ_n/δ_n=β_nμ_n↓ as product of nonnegative nonincreasing sequences. (Case 2: β_n↑, μ_n↑) δ_n=β_nμ_n ⇒ μ_n/δ_n=1/β_n↓ since β_n↑ and β_n>0, β_n/δ_n=1/μ_n↓, β_nμ_n/δ_n=1 constant. (Case 3: β_n↓, μ_n↑) δ_n=μ_n ⇒ μ_n/δ_n=1 constant, β_n/δ_n=β_n/μ_n↓ (numerator↓, denominator↑, both positive), β_nμ_n/δ_n=β_n↓. (Case 4: β_n↑, μ_n↓) δ_n=β_n ⇒ μ_n/δ_n=μ_n/β_n↓, β_n/δ_n=1 constant, β_nμ_n/δ_n=μ_n↓.]; so we have

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left[\frac{\mu_{n+1}}{\delta_{n+1}}\left(f(x_{n+1}) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\right) + \frac{\beta_{n+1}}{\delta_{n+1}}\left(g(y_{n+1}) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g\right) + \frac{\beta_{n+1} \mu_{n+1}}{\delta_{n+1}} c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\right] \\
+ \left[\frac{\mu_n \alpha_n}{\delta_n} h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \frac{\beta_n \nu_n}{\delta_n} k(y_n, y_{n+1})\right] \\
\leq \left[\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}\bigg(f(x_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\bigg) + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\left(g(y_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g\right) + \frac{\beta_n \mu_n}{\delta_n} c(x_n, y_n)\right],
\end{array}
$$

which completes the proof.

items.name: Proposition 2.1
items.proof:
Algorithm $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$ reads

$$
\begin{array}{l}
f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \tag{2.1}\\
\leq f(\xi) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n) \quad \forall \xi \in \mathcal{X}, \\
g(y_{n+1}) + \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) + \nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1}) \tag{2.2}\\
\leq g(\eta) + \mu_n c(x_{n+1}, \eta) + \nu_n k(y_n, \eta) \quad \forall \eta \in \mathcal{Y}.
\end{array}
$$

The right-hand member of (2.1) converges to $f(\xi) + \alpha_{\infty} h(\overline{x}, \xi) + \beta_{\infty} c(\xi, \overline{y})$. [This uses: $\alpha_n \to \alpha_{\infty}$, $x_n \to \overline{x}$, separate continuity of $h$ gives $h(x_n, \xi) \to h(\overline{x}, \xi)$; $\beta_n \to \beta_{\infty}$, $y_n \to \overline{y}$, separate continuity of $c$ gives $c(\xi, y_n) \to c(\xi, \overline{y})$.] Taking the lower limit of the left-hand member of (2.1) gives

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\varliminf\{f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n)\} \tag{2.3}\\
\geq \varliminf f(x_{n+1}) + \varliminf \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \varliminf \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \\
\geq f(\overline{x}) + \alpha_{\infty} h(\overline{x}, \overline{x}) + \beta_{\infty} c(\overline{x}, \overline{y}),
\end{array}
$$

[where $\varliminf f(x_{n+1}) \geq f(\overline{x})$ follows from lower semicontinuity of $f$ and $x_{n+1} \to \overline{x}$; $\varliminf \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) \geq \alpha_{\infty} h(\overline{x}, \overline{x})$ uses $\alpha_n \to \alpha_{\infty}$, $x_n, x_{n+1} \to \overline{x}$, and lower semicontinuity of $h$; and $\varliminf \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \geq \beta_{\infty} c(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ similarly uses $\beta_n \to \beta_{\infty}$, $x_{n+1} \to \overline{x}$, $y_n \to \overline{y}$, and lower semicontinuity of $c$.]

which yields the first condition for $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ to be an inertial Nash equilibrium. The second condition is proved likewise from (2.2).

items.name: Lemma 4.2
items.proof:
The function $L_{\beta, \mu}$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. [Convexity: $f$ and $g$ are convex, and $(\xi,\eta) \mapsto \frac{1}{2}\beta\mu\|\xi-\eta\|^2$ is convex as a composition of the convex squared norm with a linear map; sum of convex functions is convex. Properness and lsc follow from the same properties of $f$ and $g$.] Its subgradient set is easily seen to verify [by the sum rule for convex subdifferentials: $\partial(\mu f)(\xi) = \mu\partial f(\xi)$, $\partial(\beta g)(\eta) = \beta\partial g(\eta)$, and $\partial(\frac{1}{2}\beta\mu\|\cdot\|^2)(\xi,\eta) = \{(\beta\mu(\xi-\eta), \beta\mu(\eta-\xi))\}$, so the product structure $\partial L_{\beta,\mu}(\xi,\eta) = \partial_{\xi} L \times \partial_{\eta} L$ gives:]

$$
\partial L_{\beta, \mu}(\xi, \eta) = \{\mu \partial f(\xi) + \beta \mu (\xi - \eta)\} \times \{\beta \partial g(\eta) + \beta \mu (\eta - \xi)\}. \tag{4.5}
$$

And notice that the conditions for $(x, y)$ to be an inertial Nash equilibrium $\mathrm{INE}(0, \beta, \mu, 0)$ are

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
0 \in \partial f(x) + \beta(x - y), \\
0 \in \partial g(y) + \mu(y - x),
\end{array} \right.
$$

[which follow from Fermat's optimality condition for the unconstrained convex minimization problems defining INE(0,β,μ,0): $x \in \operatorname{argmin}\{f(\xi) + \frac{\beta}{2}\|\xi-y\|^2\}$ iff $0 \in \partial f(x) + \beta(x-y)$, and similarly for $y$.]
which are equivalent to $\partial L_{\beta, \mu}(x, y) \ni 0$. [Multiplying the first inclusion by $\mu$ gives $0 \in \mu\partial f(x) + \beta\mu(x-y)$, which is exactly the first component of (4.5) at zero; similarly $0 \in \beta\partial g(y) + \beta\mu(y-x)$ is the second component. Hence $(0,0) \in \partial L_{\beta,\mu}(x,y)$, which by Fermat's rule characterizes a global minimizer of the convex function $L_{\beta,\mu}$.]

items.name: Lemma 4.3
items.proof:
The first two inequalities entail the third one; it suffices to multiply the first by $\alpha_n\mu$, the second by $\beta(\mu + \nu_n)$, and to add.

The proof of the first two inequalities relies on the firm nonexpansiveness property of the resolvent operators $T_f^n$ and $T_g^n$. Introduce $T_f^n = (I + \frac{1}{\alpha_n + \beta}\partial f)^{-1}$ and $T_g^n = (I + \frac{1}{\mu + \nu_n}\partial g)^{-1}$. The sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ is characterized by

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
x_{n+1} = T_f^n\left(\frac{\alpha_n x_n + \beta y_n}{\alpha_n + \beta}\right), \tag{4.1}\\
y_{n+1} = T_g^n\left(\frac{\mu x_{n+1} + \nu_n y_n}{\mu + \nu_n}\right).
\end{array} \right.
$$

Any $\mathrm{INE}(0, \beta, \mu, 0)$, equivalently any $\mathrm{INE}(\alpha_n, \beta, \mu, \nu_n)$, verifies [since adding α_n‖ξ-x‖²/2 to the minimization defining INE(0,β,μ,0) doesn't change the argmin — x already minimizes f(ξ)+β‖ξ-y‖²/2 and α_n‖ξ-x‖²/2 is minimized at ξ=x, so the sum has the same argmin x]:

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
x = T_f^n\left(\frac{\alpha_n x + \beta y}{\alpha_n + \beta}\right), \tag{4.4}\\
y = T_g^n\left(\frac{\mu x + \nu_n y}{\mu + \nu_n}\right).
\end{array} \right.
$$

Resolvent operators are firmly nonexpansive, i.e.,

$$
\langle T_f^n x - T_f^n x', x - x' \rangle \geq \|T_f^n x - T_f^n x'\|^2 \quad \forall x, x' \in \mathcal{H}. \tag{4.2}
$$

From (4.1) and (4.4) we deduce that [applying (4.2) with $a = (\alpha_n x_n + \beta y_n)/(\alpha_n+\beta)$ and $b = (\alpha_n x + \beta y)/(\alpha_n+\beta)$, noting $x_{n+1} = T_f^n a$ and $x = T_f^n b$: $\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 \leq \langle x_{n+1} - x, a - b\rangle = \langle x_{n+1} - x, (\alpha_n(x_n-x) + \beta(y_n-y))/(\alpha_n+\beta)\rangle$]

$$
\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\alpha_n + \beta}\{\alpha_n \langle x_{n+1} - x, x_n - x\rangle + \beta \langle x_{n+1} - x, y_n - y\rangle\},
$$

$$
\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\nu_n + \mu}\{\mu \langle y_{n+1} - y, x_{n+1} - x\rangle + \nu_n \langle y_{n+1} - y, y_n - y\rangle\}.
$$

Write each inner product as $\langle u, v \rangle = \frac{1}{2}\{\|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - \|v - u\|^2\}$ in the inequalities above. We then obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\alpha_n + \beta}\left\{\frac{\alpha_n}{2}\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 + \frac{\alpha_n}{2}\|x_n - x\|^2 - \frac{\alpha_n}{2}\|x_{n+1} - x_n\|^2\right. \\
\left. + \frac{\beta}{2}\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 + \frac{\beta}{2}\|y_n - y\|^2 - \frac{\beta}{2}\|y_n - x_{n+1} - y + x\|^2\right\}
\end{array}
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\nu_n + \mu}\left\{\frac{\mu}{2}\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 + \frac{\mu}{2}\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2\right. \\
+ \frac{\nu_n}{2}\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2 + \frac{\nu_n}{2}\|y_n - y\|^2 \\
\left. - \frac{\mu}{2}\|y_{n+1} - x_{n+1} - y + x\|^2 - \frac{\nu_n}{2}\|y_{n+1} - y_n\|^2\right\}.
\end{array}
$$

Rearranging the terms we obtain [collecting ‖x_{n+1}-x‖² terms on each side: the RHS contains (α_n/2 + β/2)/(α_n+β)·‖x_{n+1}-x‖² = ½‖x_{n+1}-x‖²; subtracting this from both sides gives ½‖x_{n+1}-x‖² on LHS ≤ (α_n‖x_n-x‖² + β‖y_n-y‖² - α_n‖x_{n+1}-x_n‖² - β‖y_n-x_{n+1}-y+x‖²)/(2(α_n+β)); multiplying by 2 yields the final form.]

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\alpha_n + \beta}\{\alpha_n\|x_n - x\|^2 + \beta\|y_n - y\|^2 - \alpha_n\|x_{n+1} - x_n\|^2 - \beta\|y_n - x_{n+1} - y + x\|^2\}
\end{array}
$$

and [similarly for the second inequality: collect ‖y_{n+1}-y‖² terms — the RHS has (μ/2+ν_n/2)/(ν_n+μ)·‖y_{n+1}-y‖² = ½‖y_{n+1}-y‖²; subtract and multiply by 2]

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\nu_n + \mu}\{\mu\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 + \nu_n\|y_n - y\|^2 - \mu\|y_{n+1} - x_{n+1} - y + x\|^2 - \nu_n\|y_{n+1} - y_n\|^2\}.
\end{array}
$$

Now, in the last inequality, replace $\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2$ by its upper bound given by the last one [substituting the bound from the ‖x_{n+1}-x‖² inequality into the right-hand side of the ‖y_{n+1}-y‖² inequality, and multiplying through by denominators to combine] to achieve the first two inequalities asserted by the lemma.

items.name: Proposition 4.4
items.statement: Assume $\mathcal{H}41$–$\mathcal{H}46$ (as in Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.3). The sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ generated by $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$ (in the quadratic case) is bounded.
items.proof:
As a straightforward consequence of Lemma 4.3 we have [from Lemma 4.3(a), dropping the nonnegative terms $-\alpha_n\|x_{n+1}-x_n\|^2$ and $-\beta\|y_n-x_{n+1}-y+x\|^2$ (which are $\leq 0$, so removing them preserves the $\leq$ inequality), and similarly from Lemma 4.3(b)]:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{\alpha_n + \beta}\{\alpha_n\|x_n - x\|^2 + \beta\|y_n - y\|^2\} \leq \max(\|x_n - x\|^2, \|y_n - y\|^2), \\
\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2 \leq \frac{1}{(\mu + \nu_n)(\alpha_n + \beta)}\{\mu\alpha_n\|x_n - x\|^2 + (\mu\beta + \nu_n(\alpha_n + \beta))\|y_n - y\|^2\} \leq \max(\|x_n - x\|^2, \|y_n - y\|^2).
\end{array}
$$

[The max bound follows because both RHS expressions are convex combinations: in the first, the coefficients are $\alpha_n/(\alpha_n+\beta)$ and $\beta/(\alpha_n+\beta)$ which sum to 1, so the RHS is a convex combination of $\|x_n-x\|^2$ and $\|y_n-y\|^2$, hence bounded by their maximum. In the second, the coefficients are $\mu\alpha_n/((\mu+\nu_n)(\alpha_n+\beta))$ and $(\mu\beta+\nu_n(\alpha_n+\beta))/((\mu+\nu_n)(\alpha_n+\beta))$, which also sum to 1.]

Hence $\max(\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2, \|y_{n+1} - y\|^2) \leq \max(\|x_n - x\|^2, \|y_n - y\|^2)$. [This shows the max is nonincreasing in n; in particular, it is bounded by its initial value $\max(\|x_0-x\|^2, \|y_0-y\|^2)$.] This shows that the sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ is bounded.

items.name: Proposition 4.5
items.statement:
Assume $\mathcal{H}41$–$\mathcal{H}47$, where $\mathcal{H}47$ is: $\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}(\alpha_{n+1} - \alpha_n)^+ < +\infty$, $\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}(\nu_{n+1} - \nu_n)^+ < +\infty$, and consequently the sequences $\alpha_n, \nu_n$ are convergent: $\alpha_n \to \alpha$, $\nu_n \to \nu$.

Then, for any $(x, y)$ inertial Nash equilibrium $\mathrm{INE}(0, \beta, \mu, 0)$, the sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ generated by $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$ (in the quadratic case) satisfies:

(i) $y_n - x_n \to y - x$, $x_{n+1} - x_n \to 0$, $y_{n+1} - y_n \to 0$ relative to the norm topology in $\mathcal{H}$;

(ii) $\|x_{n+1} - x\|$ and $\|y_{n+1} - y\|$ have a limit as $n \to +\infty$.
items.proof:
Adopt the notations:

$$
\begin{array}{l}
A_n = \alpha_n \mu \|x_n - x\|^2 + \beta(\mu + \nu_n)\|y_n - y\|^2, \\
B_n = \alpha_n \mu\|x_{n+1} - x_n\|^2 + \beta\nu_n\|y_{n+1} - y_n\|^2 + \beta\mu\|y_n - x_{n+1} - y + x\|^2 + \beta\mu\|y_{n+1} - x_{n+1} - y + x\|^2.
\end{array}
$$

So, inequality (c) in Lemma 4.3 reads

$$
B_n \leq A_n - \{\alpha_n\mu\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 + \beta(\mu + \nu_n)\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2\}.
$$

Whence we easily derive [noting that $A_{n+1} = \alpha_{n+1}\mu\|x_{n+1}-x\|^2 + \beta(\mu+\nu_{n+1})\|y_{n+1}-y\|^2$, we have $A_n - A_{n+1} = \alpha_n\mu\|x_n-x\|^2 - \alpha_{n+1}\mu\|x_{n+1}-x\|^2 + \beta(\mu+\nu_n)\|y_n-y\|^2 - \beta(\mu+\nu_{n+1})\|y_{n+1}-y\|^2$. The braces in Lemma 4.3(c) equal $\alpha_n\mu\|x_{n+1}-x\|^2 + \beta(\mu+\nu_n)\|y_{n+1}-y\|^2 = A_{n+1} - \mu(\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n)\|x_{n+1}-x\|^2 - \beta(\nu_{n+1}-\nu_n)\|y_{n+1}-y\|^2$. Substituting:]

$$
\begin{array}{l}
B_n \leq A_n - A_{n+1} + \mu(\alpha_{n+1} - \alpha_n)\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2 + \beta(\nu_{n+1} - \nu_n)\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2 \\
\leq A_n - A_{n+1} + [\mu(\alpha_{n+1} - \alpha_n)^+ + \beta(\nu_{n+1} - \nu_n)^+]M,
\end{array}
$$

where $M$ denotes an upper bound for $\|x_{n+1} - x\|^2$ and $\|y_{n+1} - y\|^2$; $M$ is finite in view of Proposition 4.4. [Here $(a)^+ = \max(a,0)$ denotes the positive part, and the inequality uses $\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n \leq (\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n)^+$ and similarly for $\nu$.] Define $C_n = [\mu(\alpha_n - \alpha_{n-1})^+ + \beta(\nu_n - \nu_{n-1})^+]M$, and observe that the series $\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty}C_n$ is convergent owing to assumption $\mathcal{H}47$. The last inequality may be written

$$
0 \leq B_n \leq (A_n - \sum_{k=1}^n C_k) - (A_{n+1} - \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} C_k).
$$

Hence the sequence $n \mapsto A_n - \sum_{k=1}^n C_k$ is decreasing; as it is bounded below by $-\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}C_n$, it converges. As a consequence $A_n$ converges, too.

Now the inequality above shows that the series $\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}B_k$ converges, and hence $B_n$ tends to zero as $n \to +\infty$.

Since $B_n$ vanishes as $n \to +\infty$, in particular, $\|y_n - x_{n+1} - y + x\|$ and $\|y_{n+1} - x_{n+1} - y + x\|$ tend to zero. Hence $y_n - x_n - y + x \to 0$, $y_{n+1} - y_n = (y_{n+1} - x_{n+1}) - (y_n - x_{n+1}) \to 0$, $x_{n+1} - x_n = (y_n - x_n) - (y_n - x_{n+1}) \to 0$, which proves point (i).

Further, writing $x_n - x = (y_n - y) - (y_n - x_n - y + x)$ in the expression of $A_n$ yields

$$
\begin{array}{l}
A_n = (\alpha_n\mu + \beta(\mu + \nu_n))\|y_n - y\|^2 - 2\alpha_n\mu\langle y_n - y, y_n - x_n - y + x\rangle + \alpha_n\mu\|y_n - x_n - y + x\|^2.
\end{array}
$$

The last two terms vanish as $n \to +\infty$, while $(\alpha_n\mu + \beta(\mu + \nu_n))$ tends to a positive limit. Hence $\|y_n - y\|$ admits a limit as $n \to +\infty$. [Since $A_n$ converges and the coefficient $\alpha_n\mu+\beta(\mu+\nu_n) \to \alpha\mu+\beta(\mu+\nu) > 0$, dividing by this coefficient gives convergence of $\|y_n-y\|^2$.] In view of $x_n - x = (y_n - y) - (y_n - x_n - y + x)$, $\|x_n - x\|$ admits a limit, too.

items.name: Opial's Lemma
items.statement:
Let $z_n$ be a sequence in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ such that there exists a nonvoid set $S \subset \mathcal{H}$ which verifies the following:

(i) any weak limit point of $z_n$ belongs to $S$;
(ii) $\forall \zeta \in S$, $\lim_{n \to +\infty}\|z_n - \zeta\|$ exists.

Then, $z_n$ weakly converges as $n \to +\infty$ to some element of $S$.
items.proof: Cited from: Z. Opial, Weak convergence of the sequence of successive approximations for nonexpansive mappings, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc., 73 (1967), pp. 591–597.

items.name: Proposition 2.2
items.statement:
In addition to $\mathcal{H}11$–$\mathcal{H}14$ (as in Proposition 2.1), suppose

(i) $h(\xi, \xi) = 0$, $\forall \xi \in \mathcal{X}$, $k(\eta, \eta) = 0$, $\forall \eta \in \mathcal{Y}$;
(ii) $\overline{\alpha} = \overline{\lim}\alpha_n$ and $\overline{\nu} = \overline{\lim}\nu_n$ are finite.

Then the limit $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ of any sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ generated by algorithm $(\mathrm{CA}^2)$ is an inertial Nash equilibrium $\mathrm{INE}(\alpha, \beta_{\infty}, \mu_{\infty}, \nu)$, where $\alpha$ is any number greater than or equal to $\overline{\alpha}$, and $\nu$ is any number greater than or equal to $\overline{\nu}$.
items.proof:
The proof runs along the same lines as that of Proposition 2.1. [The key difference from Proposition 2.1 is that $\alpha_n$ and $\nu_n$ are not assumed to converge, only to be bounded with finite limsup. From (2.1), for every $\xi \in \mathcal{X}$:

$$
f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \leq f(\xi) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n).
$$

Take limsup on the RHS: $\varlimsup \{f(\xi) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n)\} \leq f(\xi) + \overline{\alpha} h(\overline{x}, \xi) + \beta_{\infty} c(\xi, \overline{y})$, using $\varlimsup \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) \leq (\varlimsup \alpha_n) \cdot h(\overline{x}, \xi) = \overline{\alpha} h(\overline{x}, \xi)$ [since $h(x_n, \xi) \to h(\overline{x}, \xi)$ by separate continuity and $\alpha_n \geq 0$, $h \geq 0$]. For the LHS, as in Proposition 2.1, taking liminf gives $\geq f(\overline{x}) + \beta_{\infty} c(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ (note that $\varliminf \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) \geq 0$ since all terms are nonnegative, and $h(\overline{x}, \overline{x}) = 0$).

Thus $f(\overline{x}) + \beta_{\infty} c(\overline{x}, \overline{y}) \leq f(\xi) + \overline{\alpha} h(\overline{x}, \xi) + \beta_{\infty} c(\xi, \overline{y})$.

Now for any $\alpha \geq \overline{\alpha}$, since $h \geq 0$, we have $\overline{\alpha} h(\overline{x}, \xi) \leq \alpha h(\overline{x}, \xi)$, hence the inequality holds with $\alpha$ replacing $\overline{\alpha}$. The same reasoning applied to the second coordinate yields $g(\overline{y}) + \mu_{\infty} c(\overline{x}, \overline{y}) \leq g(\eta) + \nu h(\overline{y}, \eta) + \mu_{\infty} c(\overline{x}, \eta)$ for any $\nu \geq \overline{\nu}$. Therefore $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ is an $\mathrm{INE}(\alpha, \beta_{\infty}, \mu_{\infty}, \nu)$.]

items.name: Demiclosedness of Subdifferential (Brézis)
items.statement: Let $f: \mathcal{H} \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ be a convex, proper, lower semicontinuous function on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Then the subdifferential operator $\partial f: \mathcal{H} \rightrightarrows \mathcal{H}$ is demiclosed (or weakly-strongly closed): if $x_n \rightharpoonup x$ weakly in $\mathcal{H}$ and $\partial f(x_n) \ni u_n \to u$ strongly in $\mathcal{H}$, then $\partial f(x) \ni u$.
items.proof: Cited from: H. Brézis, Opérateurs Maximaux Monotones et Semi-groupes de Contractions dans les Espaces de Hilbert et Équations d'Évolution, North-Holland Mathematics Studies 5, North-Holland, New York, 1973.

items.name: Theorem 3.1
items.proof:
Let $(x_n, y_n)$ be a sequence generated by algorithm $(\mathrm{ACA}^2)$. Using the same reasoning as in Theorem 2.5, and with the same definition for $\delta_n$, we obtain [the approximate version (ACA²) differs from (CA²) by the tolerance ε_n: for each step we have $f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \leq f(\xi) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n) + \varepsilon_n$, and similarly for the second coordinate. Repeating the proof of Lemma 2.3 with the extra ε_n terms and then dividing by δ_n as in Theorem 2.5 yields the inequality below with $(\mu_n/\delta_n + \beta_n/\delta_n)\varepsilon_n$ on the RHS:]

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left[\frac{\mu_{n+1}}{\delta_{n+1}}\bigg(f(x_{n+1}) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\bigg) + \frac{\beta_{n+1}}{\delta_{n+1}}\left(g(y_{n+1}) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g\right) + \frac{\beta_{n+1}\mu_{n+1}}{\delta_{n+1}}c(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\right] \tag{3.1}\\
+ \left[\frac{\mu_n\alpha_n}{\delta_n}h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \frac{\beta_n\nu_n}{\delta_n}k(y_n, y_{n+1})\right] \\
\leq \left[\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}\left(f(x_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{X}} f\right) + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\left(g(y_n) - \inf_{\mathcal{Y}} g\right) + \frac{\beta_n\mu_n}{\delta_n}c(x_n, y_n)\right] + \left(\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n} + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\right)\varepsilon_n.
\end{array}
$$

In view of the definition of $\delta_n$, according to the behavior of $\beta_n$ and $\mu_n$, the sequences $\mu_n/\delta_n$ and $\beta_n/\delta_n$ are nonincreasing; hence we have

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n} + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\right)\varepsilon_n \leq \left(\frac{\mu_0}{\delta_0} + \frac{\beta_0}{\delta_0}\right)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_n < +\infty.
$$

[The inequality uses $\mu_n/\delta_n \leq \mu_0/\delta_0$ and $\beta_n/\delta_n \leq \beta_0/\delta_0$ since these sequences are nonincreasing; the sum of ε_n converges by H37.]

Adding the inequalities (3.1), as in the proof of Theorem 2.5, yields the convergence of the series

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}\alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\nu_n k(y_n, y_{n+1}) < +\infty.
$$

Let $\delta_{\infty}$ be the limit of sequence $\delta_n$ (it does converge). In view of $\mathcal{H}36$ there exists some $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that

$$
\frac{\mu_n}{\delta_n}\alpha_n > \frac{1}{2}\frac{\mu_{\infty}}{\delta_{\infty}}\underline{\alpha} > 0, \quad \frac{\beta_n}{\delta_n}\nu_n > \frac{1}{2}\frac{\beta_{\infty}}{\delta_{\infty}}\underline{\nu} > 0 \quad \forall n \geq N.
$$

[This follows because $\mu_n/\delta_n \to \mu_\infty/\delta_\infty$, $\beta_n/\delta_n \to \beta_\infty/\delta_\infty$, and $\alpha_n, \nu_n$ are bounded away from $0$, so their products are eventually bounded below by half the limiting constant.]

Hence

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + k(y_n, y_{n+1}) < +\infty
$$

and finally

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}d_{\mathcal{X}}(x_n, x_{n+1}) + d_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_n, y_{n+1}) < +\infty.
$$

[Using H34: $h(x_n, x_{n+1}) \geq d_{\mathcal{X}}(x_n, x_{n+1})$ and $k(y_n, y_{n+1}) \geq d_{\mathcal{Y}}(y_n, y_{n+1})$; convergence of the larger series implies convergence of the smaller one.]

The sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are thus Cauchy sequences in the complete metric spaces $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$. Let $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ be their limits.

Recall that, by the definition of $x_{n+1}$, we have, for every $\xi \in \mathcal{X}$,

$$
f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \leq f(\xi) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n).
$$

Taking the lower limit of the left-hand side yields

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\varliminf\{f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n)\} \\
\geq \varliminf f(x_{n+1}) + \varliminf\alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) + \varliminf\beta_n c(x_{n+1}, y_n) \\
\geq f(\overline{x}) + \beta_{\infty}c(\overline{x}, \overline{y}).
\end{array}
$$

[Note that $\varliminf \alpha_n h(x_n, x_{n+1}) \geq 0$ since $h \geq 0, \alpha_n \geq 0$, and $h(x_n, x_{n+1}) \to 0$ because $\sum h(x_n, x_{n+1}) < \infty$.]

And taking the upper limit of the right-hand side yields

$$
\varlimsup\{f(\xi) + \alpha_n h(x_n, \xi) + \beta_n c(\xi, y_n)\} \leq f(\xi) + \overline{\alpha}h(\overline{x}, \xi) + \beta_{\infty}c(\xi, \overline{y}).
$$

Hence

$$
f(\overline{x}) + \beta_{\infty}c(\overline{x}, \overline{y}) \leq f(\xi) + \overline{\alpha}h(\overline{x}, \xi) + \beta_{\infty}c(\xi, \overline{y}).
$$

Likewise we can prove

$$
g(\overline{y}) + \mu_{\infty}c(\overline{x}, \overline{y}) \leq g(\eta) + \overline{\nu}k(\overline{y}, \eta) + \mu_{\infty}c(\overline{x}, \eta) \quad \forall \eta \in \mathcal{Y}.
$$

And that shows that $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ is an inertial Nash equilibrium $\mathrm{INE}(\overline{\alpha}, \beta_{\infty}, \mu_{\infty}, \overline{\nu})$.

items.name: Theorem 4.1
items.proof:
Recall that the sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are characterized by

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
0 \in \partial f(x_{n+1}) + \alpha_n(x_{n+1} - x_n) + \beta(x_{n+1} - y_n), \\
0 \in \partial g(y_{n+1}) + \mu(y_{n+1} - x_{n+1}) + \nu_n(y_{n+1} - y_n).
\end{array} \right.
$$

(a) Let $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ be a weak limit point of the bounded sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ (recall Proposition 4.4).

To simplify the notation we suppose for a while that the whole sequence converges. On the one hand $y_n - x_n$ weakly converges to $\bar{y} - \bar{x}$; on the other hand $y_n - x_n$ strongly converges to $y - x$ for any $(x, y)$ inertial Nash equilibrium (Proposition 4.5). Hence $y_n - x_n$ strongly converges to $\bar{y} - \bar{x}$ indeed. [The uniqueness of the limit in both weak and strong topologies forces equality.] Now $x_{n+1}$ satisfies

$$
0 \in \partial f(x_{n+1}) + \beta(x_{n+1} - y_{n+1}) + \alpha_n(x_{n+1} - x_n) + \beta(y_{n+1} - y_n).
$$

[This is obtained by adding and subtracting $\beta y_{n+1}$ to the first optimality condition: $\beta(x_{n+1} - y_n) = \beta(x_{n+1} - y_{n+1}) + \beta(y_{n+1} - y_n)$.]

From Proposition 4.5 we know that $x_{n+1} - x_n$ and $y_{n+1} - y_n$ strongly converge to $0$; hence $\beta(x_{n+1} - y_{n+1}) + \alpha_n(x_{n+1} - x_n) + \beta(y_{n+1} - y_n)$ strongly converges to $\beta(\bar{x} - \bar{y})$ [since $\alpha_n$ is bounded, $\alpha_n(x_{n+1}-x_n) \to 0$ strongly, and $x_{n+1} - y_{n+1} \to \bar{x} - \bar{y}$ strongly by Proposition 4.5(i)]. Owing to the weak-strong closedness of the subgradient operator [ext_thm_1: $\partial f$ is demiclosed — $x_{n+1} \rightharpoonup \bar{x}$ weakly and $\partial f(x_{n+1}) \ni -\beta(x_{n+1}-y_{n+1}) - \alpha_n(x_{n+1}-x_n) - \beta(y_{n+1}-y_n) \to -\beta(\bar{x}-\bar{y})$ strongly, so $\partial f(\bar{x}) \ni -\beta(\bar{x}-\bar{y})$, i.e., $0 \in \partial f(\bar{x}) + \beta(\bar{x} - \bar{y})$], we have

$$
0 \in \partial f(\bar{x}) + \beta(\bar{x} - \bar{y}).
$$

Likewise we can prove

$$
0 \in \partial g(\bar{y}) + \mu(\bar{y} - \bar{x}).
$$

So far we have proved only that any weak limit point $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ of the sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ is an inertial Nash equilibrium. But from Proposition 4.5 we know that $\|x_n - x\|$ and $\|y_n - y\|$ have a limit for any $(x, y)$ which is an inertial Nash equilibrium. Opial's lemma (with $\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$, $z_n = (x_n, y_n)$ and $S$ denoting the set of inertial Nash equilibrium $\mathrm{INE}(0, \beta, \mu, 0)$) then shows that the whole sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ weakly converges to an inertial Nash equilibrium.

[Verification of Opial's lemma conditions: (i) we just proved every weak limit point of $(x_n, y_n)$ belongs to $S = \mathrm{INE}(0,\beta,\mu,0)$; (ii) for any $(x,y) \in S$, Proposition 4.5(ii) gives convergence of $\|x_n-x\|$ and $\|y_n-y\|$, hence $\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2 = \|x_n-x\|^2 + \|y_n-y\|^2$ converges. Therefore Opial's lemma implies $(x_n,y_n)$ weakly converges to some $(\overline{x},\overline{y}) \in S$.]

(b) The sequence $(x_n, y_n)$ verifies

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l}
0 \in \partial(\mu f)(x_{n+1}) + \mu\beta(x_{n+1} - y_{n+1}) + u_n, \\
0 \in \partial(\beta g)(y_{n+1}) + \beta\mu(y_{n+1} - x_{n+1}) + v_n,
\end{array} \right.
$$

where we have put $u_n = \mu\alpha_n(x_{n+1} - x_n) + \mu\beta(y_{n+1} - y_n)$ and $v_n = \beta\nu_n(y_{n+1} - y_n)$. [These are obtained by multiplying the earlier optimality conditions by $\mu$ and $\beta$ respectively, and decomposing $\mu\beta(x_{n+1}-y_n) = \mu\beta(x_{n+1}-y_{n+1}) + \mu\beta(y_{n+1}-y_n)$.] In view of (4.5) this means that $(-u_n, -v_n)$ is a subgradient of $L_{\beta, \mu}$ at point $(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})$. [Because $\partial L_{\beta,\mu}(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})$ has first component $\mu\partial f(x_{n+1}) + \beta\mu(x_{n+1}-y_{n+1})$ and second component $\beta\partial g(y_{n+1}) + \beta\mu(y_{n+1}-x_{n+1})$; the inclusions above say $\mu\partial f(x_{n+1}) + \beta\mu(x_{n+1}-y_{n+1}) \ni -u_n$ and $\beta\partial g(y_{n+1}) + \beta\mu(y_{n+1}-x_{n+1}) \ni -v_n$.] Hence, for all $(\xi, \eta) \in \mathcal{H} \times \mathcal{H}$ we have [by the subgradient inequality for convex $L_{\beta,\mu}$: $L_{\beta,\mu}(\xi,\eta) \geq L_{\beta,\mu}(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) + \langle (-u_n,-v_n), (\xi,\eta) - (x_{n+1},y_{n+1})\rangle$]

$$
L_{\beta, \mu}(\xi, \eta) \geq L_{\beta, \mu}(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) - \langle u_n, \xi - x_{n+1}\rangle - \langle v_n, \eta - y_{n+1}\rangle,
$$

but $u_n$ and $v_n$ vanish relative to the norm topology of $\mathcal{H}$ as $n \to +\infty$ [since $x_{n+1}-x_n \to 0$, $y_{n+1}-y_n \to 0$ by Proposition 4.5(i), and $\alpha_n$, $\nu_n$ are bounded]. Let $(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$ be the weak limit of $(x_n, y_n)$; we then have [taking liminf of the inequality above and using weak lower semicontinuity of the convex function $L_{\beta,\mu}$: $\varliminf L_{\beta,\mu}(x_n, y_n) \geq L_{\beta,\mu}(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$]

$$
L_{\beta, \mu}(\xi, \eta) \geq \overline{\lim}L_{\beta, \mu}(x_n, y_n) \geq \varliminf L_{\beta, \mu}(x_n, y_n) \geq L_{\beta, \mu}(\overline{x}, \overline{y}).
$$

[This shows $L_{\beta,\mu}(\overline{x},\overline{y}) = \inf L_{\beta,\mu}$, i.e., $(\overline{x},\overline{y})$ is a minimizer, and $L_{\beta,\mu}(x_n,y_n) \to L_{\beta,\mu}(\overline{x},\overline{y})$, so $(x_n,y_n)$ is a minimizing sequence.]

(c) The strong convergence $y_n - x_n \to \overline{y} - \overline{x}$ has been proved in Proposition 4.5. From point (b) just above we know that $L_{\beta, \mu}(x_n, y_n) = \mu f(x_n) + \beta g(y_n) + \frac{1}{2}\|x_n - y_n\|^2 \to L_{\beta, \mu}(\overline{x}, \overline{y})$. Hence we have

$$
\mu f(x_n) + \beta g(y_n) \to \mu f(\overline{x}) + \beta g(\overline{y}), \quad n \to +\infty. \tag{4.6}
$$

Further,

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\varlimsup\mu f(x_n) \leq \overline{\lim}(\mu f(x_n) + \beta g(y_n)) + \overline{\lim}(-\beta g(y_n)) \\
\leq \mu f(\overline{x}) + \beta g(\overline{y}) - \varliminf\beta g(y_n) \\
\leq \mu f(\overline{x}),
\end{array}
$$

where the last inequality results from the lower semicontinuity of $g$ [which gives $\varliminf g(y_n) \geq g(\overline{y})$]. Now the lower semicontinuity of $f$ gives $\varlimsup f(x_n) \leq f(\overline{x}) \leq \varliminf f(x_n)$. [Since $f$ is lsc, $\varliminf f(x_n) \geq f(\overline{x})$, and together with $\varlimsup f(x_n) \leq f(\overline{x})$ this forces $\lim f(x_n) = f(\overline{x})$.] Finally, with (4.6) we have $g(y_n) \to g(\overline{y})$. [Since $\mu f(x_n) \to \mu f(\overline{x})$ and $\mu f(x_n) + \beta g(y_n) \to \mu f(\overline{x}) + \beta g(\overline{y})$, subtracting gives $\beta g(y_n) \to \beta g(\overline{y})$; with $\beta > 0$ this yields $g(y_n) \to g(\overline{y})$.]

items.name: Remark 4.1
items.statement:
Condition $\mathcal{H}47$ is but one of various assumptions leading to Theorem 4.1. Indeed, the crux of the matter is inequality (c) of Lemma 4.3. Let $(ho_n)$ be a given positive sequence bounded away from zero. Divide each member of inequality (c) in Lemma 4.3 by $ho_n$. items.name: Joint proximal algorithm
items.statement: The joint proximal algorithm minimizes the joint objective of equation (3.2) at every iteration.

items.name: Weak-strong closedness of the convex subdifferential
items.statement: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex extended-real-valued function on a Hilbert space, its subdifferential graph is sequentially closed for weak convergence of points and strong convergence of subgradients.
items.proof: Cited from: standard maximal-monotonicity closedness of the convex subdifferential.
